title: The Complete Guide to Bathroom Floor Tiling in South Africa
subtitle: From ceramic to porcelain — what every homeowner needs to know before laying bathroom tiles
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Bathroom floors take the most abuse in any home
problemBody: Bathroom floors endure daily moisture, temperature swings, heavy foot traffic, and dropped toiletries. Poorly laid tiles lift, crack, or harbour mould beneath the surface. DIY attempts often fail because proper subfloor prep, waterproofing membrane, and expansion gaps are sacrificed for speed. The result: costly re-dos within 18 months.
bouulSolution: Bouul connects you with NHBRC-registered tilers who assess your subfloor and recommend the right tile grade for wet areas
All matched tilers include a waterproofing membrane in their quote — no hidden extras for the wet-room seal
Work is backed by Bouul Escrow so you only release payment after inspecting the finished grout lines and evenness
partsNeeded: Porcelain or ceramic floor tiles (grade PEI 4+ recommended for bathrooms)
Cement-based or epoxy grout (epoxy for wet areas)
Waterproofing membrane (e.g. Weber Waterproof or SikaSeal)
Tile spacers (2–3 mm for floor), notched trowel, tile cutter
guidePricing: R 8,500 – R 15,000 for a standard 4 m² bathroom floor including labour, waterproofing, and grouting. Premium porcelain with rectified edges adds R 2,000–R 4,000.
timeline: 1–2 days for a 4 m² floor. Demolition of old tiles adds one day. Grout must cure 24 hours before foot traffic.
aiPromptExample: Tell me how to choose between ceramic and porcelain tiles for a small bathroom in Johannesburg. I have underfloor heating pipes already laid.
aiDiagnosisOutput: Ceramic is more affordable (from R 99/m²) but less dense. Porcelain (from R 180/m²) resists moisture better and supports underfloor heating more efficiently. For bathrooms, porcelain PEI 4+ is recommended. Check that the heating pipes are at least 15 mm below the finished tile surface to avoid thermal stress cracks.
escrowGuarantee: Bouul Escrow holds your payment until you verify the floor gradient drains correctly and no hollow-sounding tiles exist. Release only once you are satisfied.
pirbStandard: SANS 10107 — The South African national standard for the design and installation of ceramic floor and wall tiles. Compliance ensures minimum breaking strength and water absorption limits are met.

articleSections.heading: Subfloor Preparation and Waterproofing
articleSections.body: Before a single tile is laid, the subfloor must be clean, level, and dry. Any moisture trapped beneath tiles leads to delamination within months. SANS 10107 requires a bonded waterproof membrane in all wet areas — this means the entire bathroom floor, not just the shower. Bouul tilers use cement-board backer units or SABS-approved liquid membranes (e.g. Weber Waterproof) and allow full cure time before tiling.

articleSections.heading: Tile Selection: PEI Rating and Slip Resistance
articleSections.body: Floor tiles in bathrooms must have a PEI (Porcelain Enamel Institute) abrasion rating of 4 or higher for durability. Slip resistance is critical — look for a coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.6 or above. Matt and textured finishes outperform polished surfaces in wet conditions. Bouul's tilers bring sample boards so you can test slip resistance with a wet shoe before purchasing.

articleSections.heading: Cutting and Laying Patterns
articleSections.body: Professional tilers use wet saws with diamond blades to achieve clean cuts around toilet flanges, door frames, and corners. Popular layouts include straight lay, offset (brick bond), and herringbone. Each pattern creates different waste percentages — herringbone can waste up to 15% more material. Bouul matched tilers include a cutting waste allowance in their quote so there are no surprises.

articleSections.heading: Grouting and Sealing
articleSections.body: Epoxy grout is the gold standard for bathrooms — it resists stains, mould, and moisture penetration far better than cement-based grout. Cement grout costs R 50–R 120 per 5 kg bag, while epoxy runs R 250–R 500 per 5 kg. The grout must be applied with a rubber float and cleaned promptly. A penetrating sealer applied after curing extends the life of natural stone tiles.

articleSections.heading: Curing, Maintenance, and Longevity
articleSections.body: Do not walk on freshly grouted tiles for at least 24 hours. Avoid heavy cleaning for 72 hours. Well-installed bathroom tiles last 15–25 years with basic maintenance: regular sweeping, pH-neutral cleaner, and immediate drying of standing water. Regrouting every 5–8 years restores the waterproof seal. Bouul escrow release is tied to a final walkthrough where checked for lipping, hollow sounds, and even grout lines.

title: How to Plan and Install a Kitchen Wall Tile Backsplash
subtitle: Subway, hexagon, or mosaic — pick the right backsplash tile and get it fitted without the stress
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Kitchen splash zones are the hardest-working walls in your home
problemBody: Cooking splatter, steam, and grease attack the wall behind your stove and sink daily. Paint peels, drywall stains, and grout crumbles. A backsplash solves this, but incorrect installation — skipping backer board, using the wrong adhesive, or neglecting to seal — means the backsplash fails within a year. Finding a tiler who specialises in wall work (different technique from floors) is harder than it sounds.
bouulSolution: Bouul matches you with tilers experienced in vertical wall installations — they use lightweight thinset and gravity-conscious techniques
Every quote specifies the adhesive type (mastic for dry areas, thinset behind stoves) so nothing gets skimped
Bouul Escrow protects you: funds release after you verify straight grout lines, no lippage, and properly cut outlets
partsNeeded: Wall tiles (subway, mosaic, or hexagon — glazed ceramic recommended for easy cleaning)
White or grey thinset mortar (modified for walls; mastic for backsplash behind sink away from heat)
Tile spacers (1.5–2 mm for subway patterns)
Trowel, tile wet saw, grout float, sponge, penetrating sealer
guidePricing: R 4,500 – R 9,000 for a 3 m² backsplash area including labour, adhesive, grouting, and sealing. Handmade or artisan tiles increase the range to R 8,000 – R 15,000.
timeline: 1 day for a standard backsplash (3–5 m²). If the countertop needs removal and reinstallation, add 0.5 days. Grout curing takes 24 hours.
aiPromptExample: I want a herringbone backsplash behind my gas stove. What tile size works best, and do I need special fire-rated adhesive?
aiDiagnosisOutput: Herringbone works beautifully with 75 x 150 mm subway tiles. Behind a gas stove, use cement-based thinset (not mastic) — mastic degrades above 50°C. A cement backer board behind the tile adds thermal protection. R 800–R 1,500 extra for the labour of herringbone layout vs straight lay.
escrowGuarantee: Funds held in Bouul Escrow until you verify aligned grout lines, properly cut electrical socket holes, and sealed edges against the countertop.
pirbStandard: SANS 10107 (wall-tile section) specifies minimum tile thickness for vertical applications and pull-out strength test methods. South African tilers certified under this standard guarantee fall-safe adhesion.

articleSections.heading: Choosing the Right Tile for Wall Applications
articleSections.body: Glazed ceramic wall tiles (6–8 mm thick) are the most practical choice for backsplashes — they are lighter than porcelain, easier to cut, and the glazed surface repels grease. Subway tiles (75 x 150 mm) are the classic choice. Hexagon mosaics add visual interest but have more grout lines to clean. Bouul's tilers carry sample boards so you can see how light catches the finish before committing.

articleSections.heading: Adhesives: Mastic vs Thinset
articleSections.body: Pre-mixed mastic is acceptable for dry backsplash areas (behind a prep sink, away from the stove). Behind a hob or gas stove, modified thinset is mandatory — mastic breaks down above 50°C. Large-format wall tiles (300 x 600 mm+) require medium-bed thinset to prevent sagging on vertical surfaces. Bouul tilers specify the correct adhesive in their quote so you know exactly what is being used.

articleSections.heading: Cutting Around Obstacles
articleSections.body: Electrical outlets, light switches, and window sills all need precise tile cutting. A professional tiler uses a wet saw with a miter guide and files any rough edges. Socket holes must be cut with a diamond hole saw for a clean finish. Bouul's matching algorithm filters tilers who list intricate cuts in their portfolio — not every tiler is comfortable with complex patterns around obstacles.

articleSections.heading: Finishing Edges and Trim
articleSections.body: Exposed tile edges need finishing — either a bullnose tile (pre-rounded edge), a Schluter-style aluminium trim, or a caulked butt joint. Aluminium trims (R 80–R 200 per length) provide the cleanest modern look. Silicone caulk (not grout) must be used at the change-of-plane where backsplash meets countertop, to allow for expansion and countertop movement.

articleSections.heading: Sealing and Daily Maintenance
articleSections.body: Grout in kitchen backsplashes should be sealed with a penetrating sealer once fully cured. Unglazed tiles (some natural stone mosaics) also need a sealer applied annually. Daily cleaning with a mild dish-soap solution and a soft cloth keeps the backsplash looking new. Avoid abrasive cream cleaners which dull the glazed finish over time.

title: Durable Outdoor Patio Tiling for South African Climates
subtitle: From sandstone to slip-resistant porcelain — the best tiles for braai areas, pool surrounds, and garden paths
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Outdoor tiles face sun, rain, frost, and bare feet — most crack within two years
problemBody: South Africa's harsh UV, summer downpours, and occasional Highveld frost decimate standard indoor tiles used outdoors. Water seeps into porous tiles, freezes overnight (in Gauteng and the Free State), and causes spalling. DIY outdoor tiling often skips the expansion joints, so tiles buckle in the heat. The result: cracked, lifted, or moss-covered surfaces within 18 months.
bouulSolution: Bouul connects you with tilers who specify porcelain pavers or frost-proof natural stone rated for outdoor use in your province
All quotes include expansion joints, a geotextile underlay, and a slope analysis to prevent standing water
Bouul Escrow holds funds until you confirm the patio drains correctly and no tiles are hollow or lipped
partsNeeded: Outdoor-rated porcelain pavers (PEI 5, water absorption < 0.5%) or natural sandstone/quartzite
Flexible outdoor thinset (latex-modified, freeze-thaw stable)
Geotextile fabric and compacted crusher-run base (100 mm minimum)
UV-resistant silicone expansion joints, tile spacer kit, wet saw with diamond blade
guidePricing: R 12,000 – R 22,000 for a 20 m² patio including base prep, tiles, labour, and flexible grout. Premium large-format porcelain (600 x 600 mm or 600 x 900 mm) adds R 3,000–R 6,000.
timeline: 3–5 days for a 20 m² area including base preparation (compacting, laying geotextile, screeding). Grout curing takes 48 hours minimum before heavy use.
aiPromptExample: My patio faces north in Pretoria and gets full afternoon sun. Tiles need to stay cool enough for bare feet and withstand sudden thunderstorms.
aiDiagnosisOutput: Choose light-coloured (cream or beige) through-body porcelain with R11 slip rating — it stays 8–12°C cooler than dark tones under direct sun. Water absorption must be below 0.5% for frost resistance. A compacted 100 mm crusher-run base with 50 mm concrete screed on top prevents movement. Expansion joints every 15 m² minimum.
escrowGuarantee: Funds held until your patio passes a water-pooling test and no cracked or hollow-sounding tiles are found. You approve the slope before release.
pirbStandard: SANS 10054 — Standard for the installation of ceramic tiles in external areas, covering substrate requirements, expansion joints, and slip-resistance classification. Outdoor tilers registered with the Tile & Slate Association SA adhere to this standard.

articleSections.heading: Base Preparation: The Foundation of Outdoor Tiling
articleSections.body: Outdoor tiling fails most often because the base moves. A proper foundation requires 100 mm of compacted G5 crusher-run, a geotextile separation layer (prevents weed growth and subsidence), and a 50 mm reinforced concrete screed sloped at 1:60 to drain water away from the house. Bouul tilers measure base compaction with a dynamic cone penetrometer before laying a single tile.

articleSections.heading: Tile Selection for External Use
articleSections.body: Only tiles with a water absorption rate below 0.5% are suitable for outdoor use in SA. Porcelain pavers are the first choice — they are dense, UV-stable, and available in slip ratings R10–R13. Natural sandstone is beautiful but needs annual sealing. All tiles must have a minimum breaking strength of 1,300 N per SANS 10107. Bouul only matches tilers who stock certified outdoor-grade materials.

articleSections.heading: Expansion Joints and Movement Accommodation
articleSections.body: Temperature swings of 25°C+ in SA summer cause tiles to expand. Movement joints must be placed every 15 m² (indoor standard is 25 m²) and at all changes of plane — where the patio meets the house wall, pool coping, or garden edging. Use UV-stabilised silicone (not grout) in these joints. A Bouul tiler will mark expansion joint positions before tiling begins.

articleSections.heading: Slip Resistance for Pool Surrounds and Braai Areas
articleSections.body: Pool surrounds must achieve R11 or higher slip resistance on the wet pendulum test. Braai areas near the house benefit from R10 minimum. Glossy or polished tiles are not recommended for any outdoor wet area — they become dangerously slippery. Through-body porcelain maintains its slip rating even as the surface wears, unlike glazed tiles which lose it over time.

articleSections.heading: Cleaning and Long-Term Care
articleSections.body: Outdoor tiles need a stiff-bristle sweep and a pressure wash (max 1,500 PSI) every 2–3 months to prevent moss and algae buildup. Use a pH-neutral outdoor tile cleaner — vinegar and bleach damage epoxy grout over time. Reseal natural stone tiles annually before winter. A well-maintained outdoor tiled patio lasts 20+ years in the South African climate.

title: Professional Porcelain Tile Cutting: Tools, Techniques, and Costs
subtitle: Why cutting porcelain is harder than ceramic and why a pro is worth the rate
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Porcelain is twice as hard as ceramic — DIY cutting is a recipe for waste
problemBody: Porcelain tiles have a Mohs hardness of 7–8 (ceramic is 5–6). A standard manual tile cutter shatters them. Using an angle grinder without water cooling produces heat cracks. Homeowners who try DIY cutting typically waste 30–50% of their tiles on chipped edges and snapped pieces. Even finding a tiler who owns the right equipment — a bridge saw with continuous diamond blades and water feed — is not guaranteed.
bouulSolution: Bouul matches you only with tilers who list bridge saw or wet-saw porcelain cutting in their verified equipment profile
All quotes include waste allowance (typically 10–15% for straight, 15–20% for diagonal/herringbone)
Bouul Escrow covers you if the tiler damages more tiles than the agreed waste percentage — replacements are on them
partsNeeded: Porcelain tiles (rectified edges preferred for minimal grout lines)
Continuous-rim diamond blade (turbo or segmented for wet cutting)
Bridge wet saw or rail wet saw with water drip system
Angle grinder with diamond-cutting disc, polishing pads, safety goggles, hearing protection
guidePricing: R 3,500 – R 7,000 for precision cutting of 15–20 m² of large-format porcelain tiles. This covers labour, blade wear, and water supply. If the tiler brings their own bridge saw to site, no extra charge.
timeline: Cutting is done during installation — add 0.5–1 day to the main tiling timeline for a 20 m² porcelain floor project.
aiPromptExample: I want 600 x 600 mm rectified porcelain tiles laid on a 45-degree diagonal. How many extra tiles do I need for cutting waste?
aiDiagnosisOutput: Diagonal layout with rectified 600 x 600 mm tiles creates approximately 18–22% waste (vs 10% for straight lay). You need 7–8 m² of spare tiles for a 40 m² room. Rectified edges allow 1.5 mm grout lines. Each cut must be done on a bridge wet saw at 2,800+ RPM with a continuous diamond blade. Budget R 1,500–R 2,500 extra for the diagonal layout labour.
escrowGuarantee: Bouul Escrow holds your payment until every visible cut edge is clean, no chips larger than 2 mm are present, and cutting waste stays within the agreed percentage.
pirbStandard: SANS 10107 Section 9 — Tolerances for cut edges and visible finish. The standard requires cut edges visible in the finished installation to have a chipped edge depth no greater than 2 mm when measured by a calibrated straight edge.

articleSections.heading: Why Porcelain Requires Specialist Equipment
articleSections.body: Porcelain tile body density is 2.3–2.5 g/cm³ compared to ceramic's 1.8–2.0 g/cm³. This density means a standard manual tile cutter cannot score deep enough to snap cleanly — the tile fractures unpredictably. A bridge wet saw with a continuous diamond blade running at 2,800–3,500 RPM and a water drip eliminates heat buildup and vibration chipping. Bouul only connects tilers who own or have immediate access to proper porcelain-capable equipment.

articleSections.heading: Types of Cuts: L-Cuts, Mitres, and Holes
articleSections.body: L-cuts (around door frames) require two overlapping wet-saw passes. Mitre cuts (45-degree) are needed for skirting or corner trims — these demand a tilting bridge saw head. Round holes for plumbing pipes are best cut with a diamond core drill bit (25–40 mm). Clean holes for toilet flanges need a 100–110 mm core bit. Each specialty cut adds 5–10 minutes per tile compared to straight cuts.

articleSections.heading: Waste Management and Tile Yield Planning
articleSections.body: Calculate the number of full tiles first, then add the waste allowance. Straight lay = 10% waste, offset brick bond = 12–15%, herringbone = 15–20%, diagonal = 18–22%. Order all tiles from the same dye-lot to avoid colour variation between boxes. Bouul tilers perform a dry layout before cutting to optimise tile placement and minimise waste.

articleSections.heading: Safety and Dust Control
articleSections.body: Crystalline silica dust from cutting porcelain is a Group 1 carcinogen. Wet cutting with a water drip suppresses 85–95% of airborne silica. Tilers must use a P3 respirator when dry-cutting is unavoidable. Bouul's matched tilers are verified to use wet-cut methods — dry cutting is not permitted on Bouul-platform projects.

articleSections.heading: Cost Implications of Rectified vs Non-Rectified Edges
articleSections.body: Rectified tiles (factory-cut to exact dimensions) cost 15–30% more but allow 1.5–2 mm grout lines instead of 3–5 mm. This reduces grout usage by 40% and creates a cleaner modern look. Non-rectified tiles require wider grout lines to hide size variation and are cheaper (R 120–R 180/m² vs R 180–R 300/m² for rectified). The tiler's cutting approach does not change, but rectified edges reduce the visible impact of any minor cutting imperfections.

title: Underfloor Heating and Tiling: Complete Installation Guide
subtitle: Electric mats, water loops, and tile compatibility — everything for a warm South African winter
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Heated floors are becoming popular in SA, but the tile-over-heating layer fails often
problemBody: Electric underfloor heating mats and hydronic (water) systems shift and crack tiles above them if the wrong adhesive is used or the heating is turned on too soon. Many South African tilers are not trained in the multi-layer substrate required — SANS-compliant decoupling membrane, flexible thinset, and a controlled curing schedule. Skipping any step causes tiles to delaminate within the first year.
bouulSolution: Bouul matches you with tilers specifically trained in underfloor-heating tile installation, verified through platform references
Quotes include a decoupling membrane and flexible adhesive in the line-items — no hidden add-ons
Bouul Escrow holds payment until you verify the floor has completed the full 14-day curing cycle without any hollow spots
partsNeeded: Porcelain tiles (PEI 4+, thermal conductivity 1.0+ W/mK — avoid thick natural stone which insulates heat)
Flexible cementitious adhesive (SANS 10107 Class C2 S1 minimum for heated substrates)
Decoupling membrane (e.g. Schluter-DITRA or Weber Decoupling Mat)
Electric heating mat (e.g. Warmup or Devi) or hydronic loops with manifold, thermostat, and temperature probe
guidePricing: R 14,000 – R 25,000 for a 10 m² bathroom with electric underfloor heating mat, decoupling layer, ceramic tiles, labour, and thermostat. Hydronic systems start at R 35,000 for a larger open-plan area.
timeline: 7–14 days total. Mat installation and tile screed: 2 days. Tile installation: 1–2 days. Critical 14-day adhesive cure before turning the heating on — no exceptions.
aiPromptExample: I'm installing electric underfloor heating in a 6 m² ensuite. Can I screw into the floor to install a toilet pan after the mat is laid?
aiDiagnosisOutput: No — never screw through a heating mat. Repair requires lifting tiles and replacing the mat section (R 3,000+ repair cost). Use a floor-standing toilet pan instead of a wall-hung one, or plan the toilet position before laying the mat. If a wall-hung toilet is essential, the installer must cut the mat carefully around floor fixings and test resistance after each step.
escrowGuarantee: Funds released only after the heating system is tested (resistance test for electric, pressure test for hydronic) AND the tile adhesive has cured for the full 14-day period. Bouul sends a reminder when it is safe to switch on.
pirbStandard: SANS 10107 Appendix G — Tile installation over heated substrates. Specifies minimum adhesive class (C2 S1), mandatory decoupling layer, and the 14-day ambient cure before commissioning the heating system.

articleSections.heading: System Types: Electric Mats vs Hydronic Loops
articleSections.body: Electric underfloor heating uses resistance mats or cables (120–200 W/m² output) and is best for single rooms under 15 m². Hydronic (water-based) systems are more efficient for areas above 15 m² but require a heat pump or gas boiler and are more invasive to install. Bouul tilers can advise on which system your tile selection pairs best with — some large-format tiles transfer electric heat more effectively than others.

articleSections.heading: The Decoupling Membrane Is Not Optional
articleSections.body: Heating mats and thin-set expand differently than tiles. A decoupling membrane (e.g. Schluter DITRA) absorbs the shear movement so tiles do not crack. Cost: R 180–R 350 per m² installed. Bouul quotes always itemise the decoupling membrane. If a tiler suggests skipping it, Bouul will not process the match — it is a guaranteed failure within 24 months.

articleSections.heading: Tile Adhesive Requirements for Heated Floors
articleSections.body: Standard tile adhesive cannot tolerate the thermal cycling of heated floors. Only SANS 10107 Class C2 S1 adhesive is suitable — it maintains 1.5 N/mm² bond strength after 100 heat cycles. The adhesive bed must be a minimum of 3 mm (notched trowel 6 mm) to ensure full coverage and eliminate air pockets which cause hot spots.

articleSections.heading: Commissioning: The 14-Day Rule
articleSections.body: The cement-based adhesive needs 14 days at ambient temperature to reach full hydration (90% of ultimate bond strength). Turning the heating on earlier forces moisture out of the adhesive too fast, creating a weak bond — tiles will debond within 6 months. The start temperature must be 20°C for 3 days, then increase by 5°C per day until the target temperature is reached. Bouul enforces this schedule via escrow release conditions.

articleSections.heading: Running Costs in the South African Context
articleSections.body: Electric underfloor heating costs approximately R 2.50–R 4.50 per hour for a 10 m² bathroom at Eskom rates (R/kWh varies by municipality — City of Cape Town R 2.61, Johannesburg City Power R 2.90 as of Q1 2026). Hydronic systems with a heat pump cost roughly half to run but have higher upfront installation costs. A programmable thermostat (R 800–R 2,000 installed) reduces usage by scheduling pre-heating only when needed.

title: Grout Repair and Regrouting: Restoring Your Tiles Without Replacing Them
subtitle: Cracked, missing, or mouldy grout is fixable — and cheaper than retiling
author: Bouul Home Services Team
problemHeadline: Grout fails long before tiles do — and failing grout damages tiles
problemBody: Cement-based grout is porous. In South African bathrooms and kitchens, constant moisture, cleaning chemicals, and thermal cycling cause grout to crack, crumble, or grow black mould within 3–5 years. Once grout fails, water seeps beneath tiles, rotting substrate, loosening adhesion, and eventually causing tiles to lift. Many homeowners think they need to retile when professional regrouting saves 70%+ of the cost.
bouulSolution: Bouul connects you with tilers who specialise in regrouting — they use diamond-blade grinders to remove old grout without chipping tile edges
All regrouting quotes specify whether epoxy or cement grout will be used, and include a sealer in the price
Bouul Escrow holds payment until you confirm the new grout is even, colour-consistent, and fully cured without cracks
partsNeeded: Epoxy grout (recommended for wet areas) or cement-based grout (for walls away from moisture)
Grout saw or multi-tool with diamond carbide grout-removal blade
Grout float, rubber finishing tool, microfibre sponges
Penetrating sealer (for cement grout) and pH-neutral grout cleaner
guidePricing: R 3,500 – R 8,000 for regrouting a standard 4 m² bathroom floor and shower walls. Epoxy grout adds R 1,500–R 3,000. Individual grout spot repairs: R 400–R 800 per linear metre.
timeline: 1–2 days for a 4 m² bathroom. Old grout removal takes longer than applying new grout. Epoxy grout take 24 hours to cure before sealing.
aiPromptExample: The grout between my shower floor tiles has black mould that returns every week even after scrubbing with bleach. Do I need to regrout or just reseal?
aiDiagnosisOutput: Black mould inside the grout body means the grout has become porous and absorbed organic matter to its full depth — bleach only bleaches the surface. Regrouting with epoxy grout is the permanent solution. Epoxy is non-porous and mould cannot grow through it. Cost: R 3,500–R 6,000 for a 2 m² shower floor. Alternatively, a grout stain/sealer (R 800–R 1,500) buys 6–12 months before the mould returns.
escrowGuarantee: Bouul Escrow holds your payment until you verify colour consistency across the regrouted area and that the new grout is crack-free after a 48-hour curing period.
pirbStandard: SANS 10107 Section 10.3 — Grout joint widths and repair standards. Specifies minimum joint width (1.5 mm interior, 3 mm exterior) and acceptable methods for partial-depth vs full-depth regrouting. Full-depth removal is required when moisture has penetrated to the substrate.

articleSections.heading: When to Regrout vs Replace Tiles
articleSections.body: If the tiles themselves are intact and well-adhered (no hollow sounds when tapped), regrouting is the right call. Signs that only regrout is needed: cracked grout lines, missing grout in spots, surface mould that returns after cleaning, or grout that has pulled away from tile edges. If tiles are loose, cracked, or the substrate is water-damaged (soft or rotting), full replacement may be necessary. Bouul's tilers offer a free inspection to distinguish the two cases.

articleSections.heading: Grout Removal Techniques
articleSections.body: Manual grout saws work for small areas but risk chipping tile edges. Professional tilers use oscillating multi-tools with carbide-tipped blades or diamond-blade angle grinders with a depth-stop — the blade guard prevents tile edge damage. The old grout must be removed to at least half the tile thickness (minimum 3 mm depth) for new grout to bond correctly. Grout dust is silica-rich; Bouul tilers use shrouded tools with HEPA vacuum attachments.

articleSections.heading: Cement Grout vs Epoxy Grout – Which to Choose
articleSections.body: Cementitious grout is affordable (R 50–R 120 per 5 kg) and easier to apply, but requires annual sealing and is porous. Epoxy grout (R 250–R 500 per 5 kg) is waterproof, stain-proof, and mould-proof — ideal for showers, bathrooms, and kitchen splashbacks. It is harder to work with (sets in 30 minutes) and costs more, but lasts 10–15 years without maintenance. For any wet area, Bouul recommends epoxy grout.

articleSections.heading: Colour Matching and Design Considerations
articleSections.body: Grout colour dramatically changes a tiled surface — light grout makes tiles appear larger and cleaner; dark grout hides dirt and creates a grid-like contrast. If you are regrouting a section, finding an exact colour match for cement grout is difficult because existing grout has aged and discoloured. Epoxy grout colours are more consistent over time. Many tilers offer 30+ colour samples so you can test next to your existing tiles before finalising the colour.

articleSections.heading: Post-Regrouting Care and Sealing
articleSections.body: Cement-based grout must be sealed 72 hours after application using a penetrating impregnating sealer (water-based, R 200–R 600 per litre). Reseal every 12–18 months in bathrooms, 24 months in dry areas. Epoxy grout does not need sealing. In both cases, wait 7 days before exposing regrouted areas to heavy moisture (showering) and use a squeegee after each shower to extend grout life.

articleSections.heading: Cost Comparison: Regrouting vs Full Retiling
articleSections.body: Regrouting a 4 m² bathroom floor costs R 3,500–R 8,000, versus R 12,000–R 25,000 for full retiling including demolition and disposal. Over a 3-bedroom house, regrouting all wet areas costs R 12,000–R 25,000, versus R 60,000–R 120,000 for full replacement. Regrouting also avoids the dust, disruption, and 3–5 days of bathroom unavailability that retiling involves.
